title: UPDATE and DELETE
description: Modify and remove existing data safely. Learn UPDATE with SET and WHERE, DELETE with proper filtering, and how transactions protect your changes.

data.text: UPDATE modifies existing rows. DELETE removes them. Both are powerful — and dangerous if you forget the WHERE clause. This lesson shows the safe patterns.

data.title: Update syntax
data.code:
UPDATE table_name
SET    column1 = value1,
       column2 = value2
WHERE  search_condition;

data.title: Update from the source markdown example
data.code:
-- Set updated_at to current timestamp for all rows
UPDATE sales.taxes
SET    updated_at = GETDATE();

-- Increase max_local_tax_rate by 2% for states where it is 1%
UPDATE sales.taxes
SET    max_local_tax_rate = max_local_tax_rate + 0.02,
       avg_local_tax_rate = avg_local_tax_rate + 0.01
WHERE  max_local_tax_rate = 0.01;

data.title: Always start with a SELECT
data.text: Before running an UPDATE or DELETE, test your WHERE clause with a SELECT. Run 'SELECT COUNT(*) ... WHERE ...' to see exactly how many rows will be affected. It is far cheaper than rolling back a bad update.
You can update columns using values from a joined table. The syntax places the JOIN in the same position as a SELECT JOIN, followed by SET.

data.title: Update using a JOIN
data.code:
UPDATE p
SET    p.list_price = p.list_price * 1.10
FROM   production.products p
INNER JOIN production.categories c
    ON c.category_id = p.category_id
WHERE  c.category_name = 'Mountain Bikes';

data.title: Delete with conditions
The deadly un-qualified DELETE
data.text: DELETE FROM table_name (with no WHERE) removes EVERY row. For large tables, use TRUNCATE TABLE instead — it is faster but irreversible. For small, selective deletions, always verify with SELECT first.
A transaction groups multiple statements into a single, all-or-nothing unit of work. Either everything succeeds, or everything rolls back — so a partial update never corrupts your data.

data.title: Explicit transaction
TRY...CATCH pattern
data.text: BEGIN TRY wraps statements that might fail; BEGIN CATCH handles the error. Always ROLLBACK TRANSACTION inside CATCH if you opened one — never COMMIT a failed transaction.

data.title: UPDATE / DELETE essentials
points: UPDATE changes rows; always pair with WHERE to limit the scope
DELETE removes rows; test your WHERE with SELECT first
TRUNCATE is faster than DELETE but cannot be filtered or rolled back easily
Use transactions (BEGIN TRANSACTION / COMMIT / ROLLBACK) for multi-step changes
Wrap risky operations in TRY...CATCH and always ROLLBACK in the CATCH block

data.text: INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE are Data Manipulation Language (DML). Every change is logged in the transaction log, which enables rollbacks and crash recovery. For ad-hoc updates in SSMS, you can manually rollback with Ctrl+Z if you did not commit — but in automated scripts, always manage transactions explicitly.
